utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On Wednesday, we are Wednesday today, I would like to say hello to Mr. Stojic, Mr. Praljak, and Mr. Pusic. I'd also like to say hello to the lawyers, the witness and all the members of Prosecution, including the people who assist us. First of all, the very short oral decision concerning the request for the addition of the Exhibit 2D 02018 to the 65 ter list G. Counsel for the Defence for Stojic, on the 23rd of February, made a request concerning the addition of this exhibit to its 65 ter list. Prosecution answered orally that it wasn't going to make any objection. The Chamber notes that counsel for Defence for Stojic didn't provide sufficient argumentation about the essential nature of the exhibit pursuant to guide-line number 8 in the decision of the 24th of April, 2008. Notwithstanding, by way of exception, and for the reasons concerning a prima facie assessment of the exhibit, the Chamber considers that it is in the interest of justice to add this exhibit to the 65 ter list of the counsel for Defence for Mr. Stojic. So this exhibit is added to the 65 ter list. Second oral decision concerning the request of time on the part of the Prosecution for the cross-examination of this witness here today. In the framework of his arrival under the 92 ter procedure, the Chamber maintains its oral decision delivered already, saying that Prosecution will have 30 minutes to do its cross-examination of this witness. Mr. Registrar, I believe you have some IC numbers you wish to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through witness Pinjuh Bruno. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit IC 00930. The list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit IC 00931. The objection list submitted by OTP shall be given Exhibit IC 00932. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, please would you stand. Could you give us your name, first name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to say good afternoon to everybody in this courtroom. My name is Ante Kvesic. I was born on the 26th of May, 1962.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your occupation or profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a doctor, a surgeon, that is my profession, and also I am head of the clinical hospital of Mostar and I have been at the head of the hospital for sometime now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Doctor, have you already testified before a court or is this the very first time that you will be testifying about events that took place in former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First time, the time in a court of law at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask you to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... that I speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Doctor. You can take your seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few explanations. Ms. Nozica is going to be asking you a few questions and after that you will be cross-examined, but perhaps in the meantime, other lawyers will also be asking you questions and the Judges, too, will perhaps ask questions. That's the first phase. And then there's a second phase, and this is connected with a 92 ter procedure that was brought up by the Defence for General Praljak, and Mr. Kovacic will ask you a few questions. And thereafter, possibly the other lawyers may have some very short questions to ask you, and OTP will have 30 minutes for his cross-examination. We don't want you to lose any time. We know you have some very precious responsibilities and that you can be here only today so we shall make every effort so that your hearing end today. I am, of course, counting on the diligence of all the parties involved so that that can be done today. Ms. Nozica, let me give you the floor immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom and good afternoon to you too, Mr. Kvesic.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd like us to go through your CV as quickly as possible from university level to the post you hold today in the clinical hospital of Mostar. Can you tell the Court when you graduated from the Faculty of Medicine?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: In 1988 in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you also tell the Court where you got your first job?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: In 1989, at the beginning of November, I started working in the Siroki Brijeg health centre in the school outpatients department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I was a general practitioner and I worked with students, regular schoolchildren's medical examinations, and from time to time, I would be on duty at the emergency ward. And that was the case until 1991 when the war began and my life changed completely, so that I went into a semi-wartime post because the wounded began coming in and I became a wartime doctor and an army doctor and a combination of all that. During 19 -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, just take it slowly because I am checking to see that everything that you say is recorded in the transcript. Anyway, you were working in the medical centre in Siroki Brijeg and was anything happening there during 1992? Did you take on a new post of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Sometime in April 1992, Siroki Brijeg was shelled by the Yugoslav Army and that morning there were seven persons who were killed and a lot of people wounded, and we were faced with that situation. They were transformed to the medical centre so we became a semi-civilian semi-medical semi-military school. And pursuant to a municipality decision, I became chief of the medical corps and we started working in a different way because we placed priority on the soldiers and the wounded, and that was the case until September, or rather the end of September.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Dr. Kvesic, regardless of the fact that I have to take care of the time but it's much more important for me and for us all that everything is recorded properly, so could you speak a little more slowly, please. You said that was the case until September 1992, now what happened then, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: On the 29th of September, 1992, pursuant to orders from Dr. Ivan Bagaric and a decision from Mate Boban, I went to Mostar and became the commander of the regional wartime hospital of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And that was at the proposal of Mr. Bagaric or was it an order?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: It was a proposal according to a decision made by the president of HZ-HB, Mate Boban, and I got papers stating that I had been appointed commander and with those credentials I went to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in the hospital in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Well, in a way I'm still -- well, anyway as a walkabout of the regional wartime hospital, I stayed there in that capacity until the 20th of January, 1994. That is to say, pursuant to a HZ-HB government decision, the hospital was proclaimed a clinical hospital of Mostar as a fledgling institution, and they started to move towards peacetime work and organisation. Although during the war as well we did function as a civilian hospital because we had patients that weren't soldier, but that was the official date when we started to work under peacetime conditions and in the way we worked in peacetime. Now, of course, the events in Mostar and around Mostar and pursuant to the Defence minister, who was Vlado Soljic at the time, a portion of the hospital staff, and it had become a clinical hospital as well, they were mobilised and we had -- and about 150 people were mobilised and remained in that capacity and continued to help the wounded and took part in covering the terrain with their medical teams and surgical teams.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What you are just talking about now, pursuant to an order from the minister, could you repeat the name because we haven't got the name in the transcript, but tell us, when was all this going on?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: The 20th of January was when the hospital was proclaimed, 1994, that is, when the hospital was proclaimed a clinical hospital as a newly formed and fledgling institution. But as the war was still going on, then the Defence minister, Vladimir Soljic at that time, took a decision or, rather, issued an order whereby part of the medical staff and non-medical staff were mobilised, and this meant up to about 150 people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Dr. Kvesic, I would like to ask you again, like the interpreters did, and also Madam Nozica also asked you to slow down and also to pause, to have the break to respect that there are interpretations for the various languages and you have to stop any time when the question is being asked and before you answer. So I would like to ask you to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You mentioned a date, the 20th of January, 1994. What was your position in the hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Up until the 20th of January, 1994, I was the commander of the regional wartime hospital of Mostar. After that date, we started a procedure for moving to a civilian hospital with a civilian director and this was done over the next few months when Dr. Zoran Rebac, who was a surgeon, came to head the hospital on the basis of a competition and job advertisement. And my function was president of the management board and I was in that post for two mandates, and then afterwards I went after specialised child surgery in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, when did you leave to specialize in child surgery in Rijeka, and during what period were you there?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: The first part of my specialisation course was in Mostar in January 1995 when I went to Rijeka to the children's clinic at the part of Rijeka called Kantrida.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I stayed there until 1998. In the spring I sat my examination, passed, and went to take up my work in the Children's Hospital and since then I've been working in the Children's Hospital of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, after 1998, did you have some other posts and functions that you occupied until 2001 or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Parallel to my specialisation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, I see you raising questions that I do not believe are relevant. You have one hour only, there a lot of documents, so keep to the basics, to the essentials. Finding out what he did in 1998 is secondary compared to what happened in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will abide by that, but this was all important to me because of the credibility of the witness, that he was head of the surgery department at the Faculty of Medicine and that he held various other posts and functions, but I will follow your guidance and stick to basics.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me please, Mr. Kvesic, when did the regional hospital of Mostar come into being and that's the one we are interested in for 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: By a decision of the municipal council of the city of Mostar, I think it was in May 1992 that the decision was passed, the Mostar hospital was proclaimed to be a wartime hospital, a war hospital. And during that time, Dr. Milenko Lugonja was appointed commander of the war hospital of Mostar. In September, that is to say, at the end of September 1992, proposed by the Defence minister Mr. Ivan Bagaric, Mr. Mate Boban, the president of Herceg-Bosna appointed me as commander of the regional war hospital, and that's when it got its new name, regional war hospital in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, after the Defence Department was founded of the HVO HZ-HB, do you know in what sector this regional hospital belonged to, the regional hospital in Mostar, what sector did it belong to?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: The Mostar regional war hospital was under the Health Sector led by Ivan Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I see, thank you. Mr. Kvesic, during our proofing session we discussed the internal setup of the Defence Department and especially the Security Sector and you said that you are not well versed in organisational matters or the legal norms and provisions, so we'll skip over that part and skip over the first document in my binder, and P 02477 is the document we are going to skip over. I'd like you to look at the next document in order. I think you have a binder, do you? May we ask the usher's assistance, he will help us out. Sir, let's take a look at the next document which is P3355. So we've skipped the first one and we are on to the second. Mr. Kvesic, this is a report on the work of the Defence Department for the period from January to June 1993. Could you take a look at page 26, please, in the Croatian version, and it is page 23 of the English. Tell me when you've found the page.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, the report for the period begins there, for the Health Sector, and that's the sector that you belonged to, that is to say, your hospital, the one we mentioned earlier on; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the next page, page 27. It is page 24 of the English where it says the following: "Within the frameworks of the health centre the following are active: The main medical corps staff, the service for caring for the wounded, the control and inspection service with its sub-services." Is that right, is that what it says there?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you take a look at page 36 now, please, which is page 35 in the English. Within the frameworks of the service for caring for the wounded --

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, I don't think I've found it yet. I have page 33 and then it skips to page 37. I don't seem to have the right page.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, could you follow the transcript, then, or, rather, look at the screen in front of you, it's on e-court where we have the service for the -- for care and attention to the wounded. Was your hospital within that service?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, the next page, 36 of the Croatian which is page 35 of the English. 35, please. It will come up on your screen in just a moment. It says: "Mostar war hospital functions within the frameworks of the regional medical centre and reserve location at Bijeli Brijeg." Is that the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's the hospital we are talking about. It had five locations in town which is why we have the reserve hospital. That was the new building that had been completed and only a part of it was operational. During the war we had our surgical ward in town in the old surgical ward, and at Bijeli Brijeg in the new hospital, so it was actually in two locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we look at page 37 in e-court, or if you could find it, but please trust me, I will read you just one passage. That's on page 36 in English. In this reporting period, from January until June 1993, it says in the report: "From the Mostar wartime hospital, the Muslim staff have fled. We are appealing to you to prohibit the departure of health workers from the HZ-HB. We have the minimum number of surgeons, a surgical team from Zagreb is helping us. In Mostar we have lost 12 ambulances, a driver was killed and four wounded." Witness, was the situation as described here?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In fact, it was even worse, but these are facts and it's quite simply that's how it was. If you want me to clarify --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead, say what you wanted to.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Well, to illustrate, before the war, the Mostar hospital and health centre had 1.150 employees. In the period when I arrived there, I found 385 people working in the hospital at five locations, and quite simply it was almost impossible to organise the service. It was a very strange time. People fled. Not just Muslims, Croats, Serbs, everybody left. Everyone who had children fled. This is just to illustrate. Mostar, for example, was so empty as a town that I saw only five or six cars driving people to work. The only other vehicles were military vehicles, soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kvesic, that's precisely what I was about to ask you. So you were short of staff regardless of the ethnicity of the staff members?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. When -- and we'll come to that later, but just to illustrate, a hospital had two operating theatres but only one anaesthesiologist at the time. It happened to be a Bosniak, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at the documents 1D 00544. That's the next document. It should be just after this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question for you. The anaesthesiologist who was a Muslim, I presume he remained there throughout, throughout the conflict, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not just that, but the person is still there and has been working there all this time. We did have assistance from various hospitals, teams of surgeons came to help, otherwise we would not have been able to function. We had several thousand wounded in that hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a conclusion to proclaim the hospital in Mostar a war hospital and it's dated the 21st of May, 1992. It signed by Jadranko Topic, president of the HVO of Mostar municipality. So before the Defence Department the hospital was declared a war hospital?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we look at the next document, that's 2D 2018. It's the next document in the binder. I'll be going through the documents now in the order they are in the binder. So this is the appointment of the commander of the war hospital of the 6th of June, Dr. Lugonja, and you said that this appointment was made by Mate Boban, the president of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was appointed by the municipal council of Mostar and the appointment was confirmed by Mr. Boban after Mostar was liberated, I think it was on the 5th of June that we entered Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kvesic, let's now go back to the period we are interested in, which is after you were appointed commander of the war hospital. Could you please tell Their Honours whether you participated in drawing up any documents together with other employees of the health department? Was there such cooperation, and did you attempt to regulate some relations which had still not been regulated in all that chaos?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation in town and the situation in the hospital was dramatic. It was chaotic. The system was falling apart. The civilian institutions were no longer functioning. Neither was the social security, so we simply tried to salvage what could be salvaged and organise life in such a way that people who had acute urgent medical needs could get assistance in a hospital. Also the epidemiological situation was very bad and the institutions were simply not functioning, so through the health department, the hospital together with Dr. Bagaric, Dr. Curic of the medical corps, we tried to do what we could. For example, we have an instruction as to how certain areas should be dealt with to avoid them becoming sources of infection and infectious diseases. You have to know that at that time there were few professionals around. There weren't many professionals in any segment, including ours. I do apologise for speaking so fast; I get carried away.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, we are all trying to slow you down. Please slow down a little, we have sufficient time for what we planned. We are now discussing 2D 00923. Is that right, Mr. Kvesic? That is the general instruction for health care of displaced persons and refugees?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you say that this in fact is a document which you drew up together with Dr. Curic, Dr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sarac as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And Dr. Sarac. And that this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aren't you getting the number wrong? It's not 2D 2019, rather?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 2D 2019, thank you. 2D 2019.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So this is the document you drew up in an attempt to regulate this area?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this letter of ours was sent around

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was sent to all those we thought could be helped by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may clarify, Your Honours, 2D 00923 is an exhibit which consisted of two documents which we separated, and the document in the binder is 2D 2019. So that it can be found under both numbers. But we have the correct document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kvesic, in the regional hospital in Mostar, after your arrival up to mid-1994, were there staff members of all ethnicities, all nationalities? And please answer slowly so that your entire reply can be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I'm proud to say out loud that from the time I was appointed commander of the war hospital to this day, I have never fired anyone from work because of their ethnicity or nationality. All the people I found working in the hospital in 1992 remained at their posts. Some of them have, unfortunately, died in the meantime. All the others are still working in the hospital. When we were trying to recruit new staff members because we were terribly short of staff, I never used the criterion of ethnicity or nationality. If I needed a doctor, I would hire the doctor who applied regardless of their ethnicity. And this also goes for nurses and other staff members.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kvesic, in this wartime period between 1993 and 1995, did you hire staff members of all ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. Let me repeat, the criteria when selecting staff members did not include ethnicity or nationality. We had 385 people to begin with, and there were about 800 at the end of the war. Nobody was ever fired because of the nation they belonged to. In 1993, I happen to recall just now, at the proposal of my lawyer we were supposed to draw up lists because a lot of people had left the hospital, they didn't turn up for work for a long time. Some of them never turned up for work. So one day we were putting all these papers in order and I signed at least 100 documents dismissing people, and I'm sure they include Croats, Muslims, Serbs. We simply had to put the documentation in order. Some of these people were later rehired when they came back to Mostar, dozens of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's clarify. At the end of 1993 you say that your lawyer in your personnel department told you that some people were not turning up for work. According to the legislation then in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina, if someone did not turn up for work for a certain period of time without justification, they had to be fired; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood the law, the lawyer told me you could stay away for five days without justification, and here it was a matter of months. We didn't do anything about it because we wished these people to come back. We didn't have enough staff, but then in the end, we did have to put this in order, according to the law. After my arrival, for several months no one received a salary, so that when money started coming in, we had to put the lists in order so that we could pay those who were actually coming to work. That was the reason why we finally had to set these papers in order and these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kvesic, in the hospital where you were working, were all citizens of Mostar treated, were some even brought from elsewhere regardless of their ethnicity or nationality?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. There were no distinctions made. Everybody who needed medical treatment was treated. The hospital doors were open to all. Everyone who needed assistance was treated in the same way. All I can say is that during the worst wartime events, and I think that Their Honours have the protocols of my hospital from that period, apart from the first and last name and the date of birth, we didn't enter any other information, either the ethnicity of the patients or their membership in a particular army or unit. We assisted everyone to the best of our poor and meager abilities at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you now look at a document, that's 2D 00968.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a list of doctors employed in wartime. Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: There were very few of us. We were desperate to recruit more doctors. The moment a doctor turned up who had the appropriate educational background, we immediately employed them. There was no competition. This is a list I can comment on briefly as regards the time when these people were recruited when they were employed and their ethnicity, and this -- for example, Ljubic Bozo was a Croat from Sarajevo. Pero Celina was Croat from Sarajevo. Benjamin Alfred Markin was an African from Ghana, a friend of mine who had been working in Jajici.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Dr. Ivan Busic came from Osijek, a Croat. Dr. Miro Klaric came from Teslic, a Croat. His wife is not mentioned here, Branka Klaric, a Serb. Then there is a Muhamed Obradovic, a radiologist; he was a Muslim. Dr. Dubravka Smajic, I think she's a Croat; I'm not sure. Gordan Galic came from Tuzla; he was a Croat. Nevenka Planinic came from Tovarnik; she was a Croat. Sumanovic Darinka came from Djakovo, a Croat. Dragan Divkovic from Tuzla, I don't know what his ethnicity is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kvesic, by your leave, this will take a long time; I think this list speaks for itself. It shows when somebody came to be employed, and you've just said they belong to all ethnicities. What does reemployed mean?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Well, this man came -- he was a psychiatrist. He came to Mostar and then, for family reasons, he changed his mind and went to Rijeka. He couldn't find a job in Rijeka so he came back. So we employed him twice in the same year. Dr. Mira Besovic left the hospital just before the war but then she came back in 1994, I think it was, and then she was taken back. She is a Muslim. She is an eye doctor and she's still working in the hospital today. So these are people who had left and came back, and we employed them again because we needed them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the next document. It is 2D 00967. 2D 00967, yes. This is also a document which gives the ethnic structure of employees for the 31st of July, 1994. Just your brief comments, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Well, it springs to view that there are more Croats than there are Bosniaks and Serbs, and I'm going to explain that very simply. Prior to the war, the situation was the reverse. However, with the advent of the war, we found people -- that people had left. Some to Belgrade, some to Germany, some to the hospital on the left bank of the Neretva, and quite simply, those were the people that we could find, the labour force that was available. I'd like to remind that you in the former Yugoslavia before the war there was what was called an ethnic key, but during the war, the key was, are they available or not. Now, of course, we try and select the best people for the job, but then we couldn't be choosers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just to clarify the situation, to avoid misunderstanding, you said that there was what was called an ethnic key before the war, that is to say, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. A proportionate representation had to be respected, and during the war you had people who knew how to work, to do their job, and now you look at -- are able to look at quality more rather than what is available, generally speaking; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, we have a brief table and it says number of personnel in the clinical hospital, and then we have the figure of 868 Croats and 152 M, that is for Muslims; right? 58 Serbs and 11 others. So that was the situation on the 31st of July, 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just let me check if it's 1994. Yes, it is, in the upper corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document which is 2D 00966. And this is a piece of information from the protocol related to the number of patients treated. And here we have two groups. We see how many Bosniaks were treated, in fact. And we have two categories. We have outpatients and hospitalised patients. And then we have figures according to the different departments and wards, surgery, oncology, and so on. Mr. Kvesic, could you tell the Trial Chamber in what way did they come by these figures in and who established who the Bosniaks were treated in this period between 1993 and 1994? Who is responsible for drawing up this table and the figures there?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: This is a list of persons who we, at your request, drew up to show that all the others were treated as well. This is an example for the Bosniaks. This is the protocol compiled through looking at the whole log-book of the hospital, protocol of the hospital, and then judging by the names and surnames, we were able to establish who were Bosniaks. That's the only criteria we had. There were no other indications, so we -- the indication we took was the name. And this showed that the hospital was open to all these Bosniaks. So I consider this to be just a technical piece of information and not anything of any vital importance because the hospital from the very difficult days when it was difficult to reach the hospital, it was open today and it was open then -- it's open today, and it's always been open to everyone for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to ask you to take a look at document 2D 00603 and then we'll look at 602 afterwards. I think that those are documents in two separate binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the usher's assistance in helping the witness, please, find those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd just like us to explain to the Trial Chamber what it is we have before us. So let's look at 2D 00602 in one binder, and then the other document in the other binder. And they are both equally important documents now. It says that this is a protocol of patients from the neuropsychiatric ward. Now, Mr. Kvesic, when we received information from you that in the neurology and psychiatry ward patients were treated as outpatients, and you say that in 2D 00966, that the figure was 814 patients who were Bosniaks. Now, can you confirm for the Trial Chamber that this, for example, is the protocol of one of those outpatient departments under the neurology and psychiatry department. And as we can see from document 2D 603 on page 1, dating from the 12th of March, 1993, that's the page, the entries go from the 12th of March, 1993, down to -- and I have to look at the next document, it is 2D 602, and look at the document at the end, and the last entry there is the 14th of March, 1995. Is that right? There was one protocol that was kept and then you continued to make entries until 1995, that's the penultimate page of document 2D 00602.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, we weren't able to get all the protocols but do the protocols exist to this day in the hospital, and can they all be verified and checked according to the different departments?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct. I'm quite sure that the list that we have in document 966 was taken from this protocol, 2D 00602, and relates to neurology and psychiatry. And I'd like to remind you that hospital protocols, complete hospital protocols, stamped and signed by me have been in this Tribunal for many years. I think it was in 1995, but don't hold me to that, during the first trial held, that is to say Mr. Naletilic, I think, they had entire protocol of the war hospital, and it's been at the Tribunal for all those years. And I still have the original version and is available for any verification that needs to be made, and I can confirm that the tables that we have here correspond to the original protocol and come from the original protocol.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the next document which is 2D 00965. Mr. Kvesic, here we have the ethnic structure of the staff on -- as of the 31st of July, 1993, in the clinical hospital Mostar. Now, previously, we had the ethnic structure as well, but that was for 1994. I'll give you the exact date. From the 31st of July, 1994. Or rather, this is the 31st of July, 1993. From this table it follows that in all the clinics there were 496 employees -- 496 Croats, 171 Muslims, that is to say Bosniaks, 66 Serbs, and 14 others. Now, Mr. Kvesic, I just want you to confirm that all these facts and figures are true and correct and that you compiled them -- that you looked through them and verified them together with your staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that absolutely. They are absolutely correct. And when I commented on the previous table, I'd like to say that the ratio looking at these figures, the 31st of July, 1993, we have 747 employees; and on the 31st of July, 1994, we have 1.089. I'm not sure I analysed that, but anyway, we tried to replenish the staff so that the hospital could function normally. But we did not have any ethnic quota system in place, and I'd like to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Now may we look at 2D 00964 next, please. This is a list of staff -- hospital staff who were killed during the war. The fatalities.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately, those are the fatalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And on that list we also have people who were Croats and Bosniaks and possibly Serbs and other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Well, let's see. I don't think there's a single Serb there. Oh yes, there is, Predrag Puzlic, one. Then there are a few Bosniak names and a few Croatian names, unfortunately, regrettably.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Kvesic, from what you have told us so far we heard that all patients coming to the hospital were treated regardless of their ethnicity. Now, were patients treated with -- did people bring patients from outside or members of the BH army who came to your hospital regardless of how they came to be in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat once again and I'll always repeat it, that without exception everybody brought to the hospital was treated at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, look at 2D 00971, please. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The document is dated the 19th of February, 1994, signed by Mr. Bagaric and it says: "We attached -- we sent you a letter we received from the International Red Cross. We ask you to act accordingly to the text. It has been agreed with the head of the Mostar hospital, Dr. Kvesic, that the mentioned patients can be brought on Monday, February the 21st, 1994, to the internal medicine ward." Your name is mentioned and we have the letter attached. Several names are mentioned there. May we have your comments? We have to look at the ethnicity of these patients, and do you remember whether they were admitted to hospital and given satisfactory medical care and attention?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Well, two things here. At that time because of the situation on the ground, in the field, and because of the inaccessibility of the terrain, because of the war, the International Red Cross drove ambulances and other ambulances and APCs, they would bring people in from the areas under threat. And that was the only reason why we reacted in this way. And I can only assume or, rather, I'm quite certain that this is correct, and you can check this out on the basis of the protocols, but I didn't verify that because I'm absolutely sure that this is correct. Now, your question as to their ethnicities, judging by the first and last names, Hasan Vasic is absolutely a -- is a Bosniak. I'm certain of that, and I'm sure that they were treated in our hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. We don't have the exact names in the transcript but we'll put that right subsequently. Look at 2D 00566 now, please. That's next document.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: 2D 00566 is the document number. That's right. Now, the date here is the 10th of September, 1993, and this is a list of wounded members of the BH Army sent from the HVO war hospital at Mostar to the hospital in Split. Mr. Kvesic, we have some names here of the members of the BH Army. The document is signed by Mr. Sandrk, and from the document we can clearly see that they were members of the BH army and that they were admitted to your hospital and that from there they were sent to Split. Can you tell the Trial Chamber or, rather, explain to the Trial Chamber why they were in your hospital and do you know that this happened and why they were then sent to the hospital in Split. But just slowly, please. Take it slowly, go ahead, yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: This list is correct, the people were indeed admitted to our hospital for treatment and because of their general health situation, that is to say, the severity of their wounds and injuries, and because we weren't able to provide medical care for a large number of people, we had very few staff and the surgical theatre was under threat, the hospital was shelled, windows were shattered, for example -- or, rather, the windows looked out on to the positions of where the attacks were coming from. So we would do what we could for these people first. Apply first aid, and then many of them, these and many others were transported to Split for further treatment. And I'd like to underline that Dr. Ivo Sandrk organised transport for them and they just happened to be members of the BH Army. But in my protocols, the ones you have here, there were many, many other people, Bosniaks and others who were transported to Split. And let me repeat, we never had a problem there. The Split hospital was also open to all patients at all times. It might be interesting to note at this point that --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a moment, everything you are saying is very valuable and interesting, but could you just slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: The Split hospital, as I said, admitted all patients and took over their medical treatment, and we had a very good experience with them, and as human beings and as doctors, Doctors Without Borders, they were -- well, if I can put it this way, they were our sort of rear hospital. We never had any problems, except for individual instances. I have a nurse working in my hospital, she was a Muslim, and she's still working in the hospital, she was pregnant and was supposed to give birth in Mostar, but as to a difficult birth she had to be sent to Split. And since she didn't have a passport, I provided her with my own car and driver and he quite simply smuggled her across the border to have her give birth in Split. And her daughter is alive and well today and goes to school. So the people could only encounter problems if they didn't have a passport. They never had any other problems. So this list, as you can see here, Mirsad, Ibro, Azer, Camir, Senad, they are all Bosniak names. And next to some of those names you have ABiH; next to others there's nothing. But as far as we are concerned, in our hospital, this did not present a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have three more documents that I want us to look at and I think that I still have 10 to 15 minutes left. Look at 2D 00328 now, please. I'll ask you some questions first. Just a brief question, general question. From your hospital from the requirements of the hospital in eastern Mostar during 1993 and 1994, did you send medicines, blood, and some other medical equipment and drugs, and did that go via the UNHCR and what was -- what kind of cooperation did you have with the doctors on the east bank?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Well, the paper that I have in my hands now refers to transporting blood for blood transfusions going to the left bank, and UNPROFOR transported this; and throughout those unfortunate years, we always communicated with the other hospital and vice-versa. So in our hospital we had a large depot of medicines and drugs and different donations from different institutions and states all over the world came into that depot. It was an open warehouse and the medicines were divided up and anybody who asked for them were sent them and we have the records of that. And just for illustration purposes, during the war, we were left without a sterilizer, which is a key instrument if you are going to do proper surgery. And then for about a fortnight we sent our surgery sets to the hospital on the left bank to be sterilized. So I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, I think you only have six minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would rather accept Judge Trechsel's gesticulations when he said eight minutes, but I'll abide by what I've been told.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I do apologise, Dr. Kvesic. You were talking about the sterilizer, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat, we sterilized our surgical sets in that hospital. So let me repeat, the hospitals always cooperated. Always. Just another small illustration, throughout the war, throughout the unfortunate time of hostilities our hospital had the only dialysis in the region and all patients who needed dialysis were brought there. Those who were from the left bank and could not be brought over slept in our hospital the whole time, as you can see in our hospital -- in our hospital records. They stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kvesic, please look at the last document in your binder. We have to skip one because of lack of time. That's 2D 0003.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 2D 00303, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please explain what the Bura action mentioned in this report -- of the medical report of the 8th of November, 1993, refers to. Let me mention that your name is also mentioned in this report. You brought blood from Split and you gave assistance near the old bridge in Mostar, but can you please say very briefly what the action Bura was in November of 1992 and who was in conflict with whom?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: It was Croats and Bosniaks together against the Serbs. The result was a disaster for all sides. There were huge numbers of casualties. I was personally introduced into this action in a way that I will remember all my life. At about 9 p.m., Dr. Goran Vojic rang up, he found me at a family celebration and he said in the morning there will be an action beginning, it's called Bura. He mentioned thousands of soldiers and I had only 8 doses of blood for transfusion. That was about 9 p.m. My car had been smashed and there were very few cars in the hospital so I borrowed a car from the Siroki Brijeg police station. I rang up the chief nurse, Mrs. Marija Zupanovic, in the Split hospital. I asked her for urgent assistance. I sat in the car, drove to Split and took from Dr. Erceg [phoen] 200 doses of blood and brought them back to Mostar. It was still nighttime. I drove without lights. It was pitch black. The silence was eerie. I left the blood there and I went back to Zovnica. I didn't have the nerve to did to my office in Bijeli Brijeg. I was soaked through with sweat, I was terrified. I smoked a cigarette there and I went back to the hospital to my job. I will never forget Bura.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kvesic, you said that this was an action conducted by the army of BH, together with the HVO, against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Before this action, do you remember that the territory of Mostar and to the south of Mostar was shelled frequently by the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Well, it's hardly worth saying that it's so obvious. Just to illustrate with an example from my hospital, you can still see the facades of the old hospital, and even the new one, there were hundreds of hits. You can see thousands of holes from projectiles on the facade of the hospital. We once had a bomb landing in our operating theatre during surgery; fortunately, it did not explode.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kvesic, to round off, we saw pictures in this courtroom showing the conditions prevailing in the hospital in East Mostar. Can you tell Their Honours briefly what conditions you worked in? Did your hospital regularly receive water, electricity? Did you have normal operating theatres? What were the conditions of work in your hospital, especially in 1993 and early 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: We had two operating theatres in two locations in the old surgery building, which we have moved out of recently. We worked in the corridor because that was in the cellar, it was an improvised operating theatre. There were lamps which we brought from outside. They weren't hanging from the ceiling, they were just lamps we used. You saw the list of dead in my hospital, 35 people were wounded. I don't think I need to talk a lot about the conditions we worked in. I think in Bijeli Brijeg the operating theatre was a bit better because it was a new building, the part that was finished. But electricity was frequently -- and especially when the situation was the worst, in spite of the fact that we had batteries and cisterns and -- well, when there were shortages, we had a firefighter staying parked all the time in front of our hospital in case we ran out of water. We lived in horrible conditions in Mostar. We weren't actually hungry but everything else, there was a shortage of.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And finally, my last question and I need the usher for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to tell you that last night we received a document which we feel to be quite important. I would like to ask for it to be put on the ELMO. We have prepared a sufficient number of copies for Your Honours. This is a newspaper which we came into our hands last night and we think it's important to mention this. It concerns a huge reward which this gentleman before us received, the witness received it. This is a newspaper dated from February 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the date, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received this newspaper last night. I will ask -- could I just put this on the transcript and then my learned friend can object.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We object because we just learned that they received this newspaper yesterday. Today, they still were modifying the list of exhibits and we didn't receive any information about this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me explain. This is not a new document. We are simply putting this to the witness so that he can confirm that it concerns him and then we shall tender it later on and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kvesic, it is a great honour to me personally to put this question to you. On the 20th of February, 2009, a magazine organised an event under the auspices of the federal television station of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and you were declared the person of the year. Can you please confirm this and explain to Their Honours whether the candidates for this prestigious title were members of all ethnicities from the entire of Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm quite surprised by this now, yes, this is correct. The reason I was nominated was a project completed by my team and myself after 18 years of work, and that's the hospital in Bijeli Brijeg of 30.000 square meters with new equipment. This hospital was opened and I'm very proud of that. That evening in Mostar some 20 people were awarded various plaques and awards and this was the last award. The readers of the magazine voted. One prize went to the prime minister and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So your work is recognised even today throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and especially on the territory of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Well, one might say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you for your responses. Your Honours, I have completed my examination-in-chief now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very quickly, I would like to ask you a question. I was looking at the document P2253, which is the list of the casualties that was established on the 10th of May, 1993, by the Health Sector for the Defence Department, and what I see is at the end the figures 162 injured soldiers, 21 Muslim -- 25 Muslims, 25 Croats killed and 2 Muslim soldiers killed and 12 civilians killed including 10 Muslims, and 11 unidentified bodies at the morgue of Bijeli Brijeg. It would have been interesting to have the same report for the end of 1993, since we are talking about the month of May. This is my question: The Muslims that were injured and taken care of in your hospital, take, for instance, the soldiers mentioned here, when they were brought to your hospital were they guarded by other soldiers, or were they considered as ordinary patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ordinary patients. I can tell you many examples where a patient was a member of the army and a member of the HVO would be on the next bed in the same room. There was no special security. We didn't even have a porter. Nobody wanted to do that. Anyone could enter the hospital. It would have been a good thing if we could have kept some things under control, but the hospital was actually open to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another additional question. Everybody knows how a hospital works, either because you have been a visitor there or you've been a patient there. These Muslims who were taken care of in the regional hospital, did they get visitors? Did their families come to visit them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no prohibitions. I believe that those who did not receive visits, did not receive them because their families were far away or it was too dangerous for their families to come. But we did not have any special regimen for one group as opposed to another. We doctors, not just Croats, but all of us doctors, we tried to salvage whatever could be salvaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last technical question. I try to keep to the essentials and be very quick. I don't need several hours to understand. I was very surprised by the document of Mr. Topic's document which refers to your clinic as being a wartime hospital. Why does Mr. Topic become involved? Wasn't it up to the Department of Defence to say whether it was a wartime hospital? What has the president of a municipality have to play as a role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of the war, Your Honour, the situation was such that we did not have any organised defence. The municipal councils carried out all activities, especially in the town of Mostar which was the largest town. It was only later that the Defence Department and the Health Sector were set up, so I can speculate now that had there been a Defence Department at the time, it -- then Dr. Rubinja [phoen] would not have been the commander of the hospital. But the municipal council was the only body functioning at the time, making decisions according to their assessments and conscience; it was simply what had to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The other counsels for the Defence and cross-examination. D 3, any questions? Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No, we do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions either. We would like to thank Dr. Kvesic for coming here to testify. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence of Valentin Coric has no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Mr. Prlic has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, the best thing now is to have a 20-minute break and then the OTP will have its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to facilitate planning, we looked at the advice you gave us yesterday, the pros and cons and some technical aspects, and we note that we can take this witness to 92 bis, take a 92 bis statement because we are pressed for time today. So to avoid any nervousness and bother, I'll do it under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. OTP you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: My name is Miguel Longone and I will cross-examine you on behalf of the Prosecution today. I would like to start showing you a video that was used with another witness here in the courtroom, Mr. Thornberry, and it is Prosecution Exhibit P04296.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, this is -- what hospital was this one?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: This was the hospital at Bijeli Brijeg where I was commander from 1992, September, until 1994. So Bijeli Brijeg is one of the localities where the hospital was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And, sir, were you present -- this specific video was from 19 August 1993 where Mr. Thornberry and this pilot were delivering medical supplies to that hospital. Were you present at that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I can't see myself on that footage. There was Dr. Bagaric and Dr. Pandza, my assistant; Dr. Simunovic, one of the neurosurgeons at the war hospital, were featured. I don't know where I was at that time. So I'm not quite sure whether I was actually there that day or not. Very often we received aid from different organisations, from UNPROFOR, the International Red Cross, the Merhamet charity, so I have to mention, because of the situation, that we functioned on the basis of donations, assistance given to us in medical equipment, sanitary material, food, medicines, and so on. So I can just use this brief opportunity to thank everybody who -- thank the hospital and -- thank everyone who made it possible for the hospital to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And I take note that you mentioned the Merhamet as assisting also there, the HVO hospital at that time, and you mentioned also in the statement that you gave to counsel for Mr. Praljak. And, sir, at that time, this is August 1993, did you ever go to the hospital in East Mostar, because you said that you were cooperating with the people in East Mostar. Did you ever go to assist them as a surgeon, to that hospital?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: At that time I wasn't a surgeon. I was an organiser and -- with management to ensure that the hospital functioned logistically. So I wasn't a doctor working with patients, but yes, I was at the hospital on several occasions. Very often, actually, because I was and have remained friends with all those people, with Minister Omerovic, Bajro Saric [phoen] who was the director, and many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: You said you went to the hospital in West Mostar, did you go at any time in 1993 in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I think it was 1994. It was very difficult to do that in 1993 without the help of UNPROFOR's APCs. So during 1993 we used UNPROFOR's vehicles and used them to help us sterilize material, but it wasn't possibly physically, not because of poor human relations but because it was because it was terribly dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: It was terribly dangerous. Sir, just to go back to the list that you have prepared of names --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for you following the video, question for you at OTP. We just saw a video, I don't know exactly what month it relates to, and we see the hospital receiving supplies. I was very much impressed that the fact that in the APC, we see equipment, medical equipment that is going to be brought to the hospital. And when I looked at the video, I wondered, well, is the UNPROFOR doing the same thing with East Mostar hospital because although the situation in the west was very difficult with this APC, they could have brought supplies to the East Mostar hospital that was facing enormous difficulties. So as far as you know, your colleagues in East Mostar, did they get supplies from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We all received supplies from UNPROFOR. We used UNPROFOR vehicles to transport supplies from us to them and from them to us. Now, at that time there were very few connections that functioned properly, but the Red Cross and UNPROFOR were used often for the transport of the wounded and material generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, you are not really answering my question which was a very precise one. I wanted to know whether the hospital in East Mostar had received medical supplies and blood, surgical equipment, gas supplies, oxygen supplies, that's what I want to know. Do you know or don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know of a number of times when from my hospital we sent supplies, medical supplies and blood to the other hospital, and various other things. Not once, several times, so I'm quite sure that that did happen. I know about the things that went from my hospital and I can substantiate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's an important thing. During what period did you send medical equipment to the East Mostar hospital, in particular blood supplies? Was it in 1993, 1994? What was the exact date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw the documents a moment ago and I think that we can find some of those dates, but I'm quite sure that there were dozens of shipments like that. I'm sure we can find a document to bear that out and tell you the exact date, but please believe me when I state this, and you can ask the director of the hospital now, that that wasn't a problem at all. So all the supplies that both

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: far as you know -- well, I think he has been a witness here already. He kept records so he has whole lists of medical supplies and blood and solutions that went to the other hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand properly, what you sent to the hospital were put into the APCs that belonged to UNPROFOR and they were the ones to take it to the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, yes. And we used that system very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Due to protective measures, could we

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: but it might appear later on. And to help the Trial Chamber, the witness was referring to document 2D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, there should be an order for page 29, line 23, in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let me be of assistance, Your Honour. What the witness was just telling you about was to be found at document 2D 00328. And the date of the document was the 25th of September, 1993. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, we discussed this document with the Defence already, it's 2D 00966, and this is a list of patients, Bosnian Muslim patients that you treated. It's a short question about it, but you have prepared -- and counsel has showed it to you and you confirmed that you made the list. And my question is the following, because this subject has arised in the past in this courtroom: Did you feel that you could make a reliable list of Bosnian Muslims being treated, Bosnian Muslims patients treated there only by -- based on their name? You felt confident in drawing that list and making sure that they were Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I stated that very clearly and I am going to repeat it now. This is a list of those people whom we recognised as being Muslims on the basis of their first and last names which in practice means that there might have been more people because lots of Muslims have names which you can't distinguish from Croatian names. For example, Zlatko Devic and so on, but for those that we were sure about, we listed and that's why the numbers were different. But in our protocols, the persons that we registered as such, I can tell you that we are absolutely certain about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Now --

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: If we see another exhibit that was discussed with the Defence before, 2D 00965, we can see that -- I don't know if you have it with you. 2D 00965. Right. So we can see, sir, for example, surgery, there are 20 surgeons that are Muslims, according to this list. This is from July 31st, 1993, by the way. And there are 20 Muslims that are -- Bosnian Muslims that are surgeons and they are under anaesthesiology that you said that it was a very important, a very, very important profession at the time because you were -- you didn't have many anaesthesiologists. You had eight Muslims. Did you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have to make a correction. These are not doctors; they are employees, the staff in the surgery department. So of these 52 Croats, 10 were doctors, for instances and the rest were nurses. Of the 20 Bosniaks, that is to say, the number of employees, I don't know what their profession was, but let me repeat at the -- in the Mostar hospital in the beginning of the conflict, we were left with just one anaesthesiologist and that was Dr. Selma Jakupovic, a lady doctor. And the others under anaesthesia were technicians, we had enough of those. And unfortunately, under the conditions that prevailed, these experienced technicians had to work as full-fledged anaesthesiologists, which wouldn't happen now but we didn't have a choice at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You mentioned that that one was Muslim actually, Bosnian Muslim, the anaesthesiologist, the only one helping you, that was what you said in the beginning of your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And, sir, if we see here, July 31st, 1993, the majority -- according to this list that you signed, the majority of employees in your hospital were Croats; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the ratio is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And in the other list from 1994 that we saw also, that the Defence here counsel showed to you, again the majority of employees at the hospital in Mostar, West Mostar, were Croats; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Now, there is something that I don't understand from your -- or I may understand from your testimony and this is you have given a testimony to counsel that -- today we were just told before starting the cross-examination they are going to tender you as a 92 ter, but in that testimony, sir, you said that at all -- not at all times but when you arrived to the hospital under from 385 employees, certainly the Croats were the minority. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And we have seen from the Exhibit P 03355 from the Prosecution under the minister of defence, the Health Sector remarks about the fact that many Bosnian Muslims employees, expert medical staff working in the Croatian hospital in West Mostar have fled, and this was a report from the first half of 1993; right? So would you agree with me, sir, that in the beginning of 1992 when there was in Mostar no conflict between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, you had a majority of Bosnian Muslim personnel working at the hospital that fled as a consequence of the war; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I said, and the information is correct, that when I arrived at the hospital I found 385 people there. Now, about 70 per cent roughly, and I have the list so you can calculate that, were not Croats. Now, what actually happened. Your observation that they went because of the war, that they left because of the war I agree in part. And here is why. I keep saying that prior to the war the hospital had 1.500 employees; that's a vast number of staff. When I came, there were 385 which means 30 per cent. Now, we tried to have people return, those who dared return, leave their children and come back to Mostar, but at the time people fled to all parts, Zagreb, Split, Sarajevo, to Bosniaks [as interpreted], the Serbs to Serbia, to Republika Srpska, wherever they could. It was a terrible time. Now, when the war broke out we managed to have some people come back and many people working today in the Safet Mujic Hospital worked in our hospital until that day; so after that day, lots of people left out of fear. It was terrible. On the other hand, you mustn't forget that because there was fighting going on the streets of the town, they had to organise the medical corps and for their own soldiers. And on one day I replaced Dr. Dzudza, who was the psychiatrist, and when the war began I wasn't a friend with Dzemal Dzudza, I was with Ramo, but he went over there. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that I have to interrupt you, but because of time constraints. I will have to do it. And I will try to ask you please concentrate on the question. The question was that: In the beginning of 1993, you clearly stated in your statement given to the counsel of Mr. Praljak, that the minority were Croats not Muslims and it's clear from the Health Sector report that the counsel --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sure you understand why I'm on my feet to object. The statement given to Mr. Praljak has not been tendered nor can it be the topic of the cross-examination so I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All that counsel can cross-examine on is the examination-in-chief material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, Mr. Kovacic sit down, please. When you answered the Prosecutor -- I'm trying to follow this closely so there's no mistake with my understanding. What I understood was this, and if I'm mistaken, please tell me immediately so that we can gain some time. As far as I understood, this hospital, before you arrived, before you arrived had 1.500 employees, doctors, nurses, various personnel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... the war. On the eve of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... miscellaneous. Now, when you arrived, there were only 385. In other words, 1.200 had left. Now, of these 385 that were there when you arrived, as far as I can tell, there are 70 per cent Muslims or non-Croats, Muslims, Serbs, whatever. 70 per cent. And I also thought that what you said was that because of the events other people left. We have a document that shows that at a certain time the figures had gone up and at that time your hospital, and I'm talking about document 2966, whether 496 people and out of these 496 they are 171 Muslims. So between the time you arrived and the time you drafted this document, 100 people more were added. But there we see that the Muslims only account for 25 per cent. 25 per cent or, rather, less, 23 per cent as compared to the 496 figure. So between the time you arrived and the time you drafted this document, lots of Muslims left. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am telling you how things stood, what things happened. When we have 496 people, several things took place. There was a new exodus of people when the new conflict began and the Bosniaks went to a new hospital which is still functioning today. So they felt the need to have their own hospital, and in the meantime, we had to look for new people. And we employed nurses, medical technicians and so on and we tried to get the system up and running without looking at whether more Bosniaks left or Croats left. What was essential for us was to fill the work post, that's what I'd like to insist upon. So that was the principle that we applied. Not by doing the maths and adding up figures. We can do that, ultimately, to see how much of what ethnicity they were, but I have documents to bear out what I'm saying. I never dismissed anyone on ethnic grounds, it was -- people fled out of fear. They needed to be elsewhere, so I understand some of the Bosniaks that left. The doctor that left. And I would have gone had I been a Bosniak. I would have transferred to the other hospital too. So those are things that happened, unfortunately. It wasn't an easy decision. If you had to leave your apartment and take your children away, the situation was terrible, but let me repeat I do not accept that the cause of their departure was a strategy to just retain Croats and dismiss the Bosniaks. That is not what happened. That was not the principle which we applied. So when you look at figures, you must look at the correlations. I don't accept that things happened in the way you've just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] OTP, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And, sir, I take two words -- two statements that you made. You just said if I would -- if you had been a Bosniak you would have gone. I would have gone if I would have been a Bosniak and I would have transferred to the other hospital, the east hospital. And I understand you, doctor. Very clearly I understand you. And just -- I'm sorry I have to be -- go very quickly through all these exhibits with you. My apologies to that. But in that exhibit that was shown to you from the Prosecution, P 03355 for 10 June 1993, the Health Sector -- this report produced by the sector under the authority of Mr. Stojic says that the medical supply was satisfactory or is satisfactory thanks to much appreciated supplies from the donations. That's page 23 of the English version, and 26 of the B/C/S. And mentioned between brackets, just underneath, there was a lack of expert medical staff throughout that year, that period. The first half of 1993. And the second page, page 24 of the English version, and page 27 of the B/C/S version, again he says that: "Another large problem is also lack of expert medical staff. Despite the prohibition for the medical staff to leave the HZ-HB, the police at the border crossings of the RH," I take it Republic of Croatia, "failed to prevent a single medical worker in leaving the area of Herceg-Bosna. Decrease in numbers of medical staff, especially of Muslim ethnicity, still continues. At the moment, we lack surgeons and anaesthesiologists and anaesthesiology technicians."
