Which is what you have told us before. Now, on the other hand, you said clearly that if you had been a Bosnian Muslim you have would have gone to the other hospital or fled. But on the other hand, as you can see here on page 25 of the English version, and I think it's page 28 -- in the top of page 28 of the B/C/S version, it says that: "All services at that time were engaged at the maximum and operating with the relatively small number of expert staff," you mentioned anaesthesiologist, the only Bosnian anaesthesiologist that you have in the hospital, for example, "which in our opinion is caused by unjustified departure of medical staff of Croatian ethnicity to the Republic of Croatia." So you justified the flight of the Bosnian Muslims but not of the Croatian people. Do you agree with this, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Let the witness respond --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: -- I'm cross-examining. Let the witness respond, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, before we hear the answer. My objection comes before the witness is allowed to answer. Your Honours, with all due respect, and I have listened carefully, had I received this question after this question which has three hypotheticals, I wouldn't know what I was being asked. Do I agree with what? What? There are four things being put forward here. So it is my suggestion that the Prosecutor breaks his question down into four, A, B, C, D, and then ask whether A is correct, Bis correct or whatever. This way it's completely non-understandable. And there's an error here, he didn't say that anybody fled or that he fled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your question was very long and I see all your sentences in the transcript and I say how will the witness understand all of this. Now, I think you need to be more concise in your questions in order for the witness to be able to answer and then you move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, my question is the following: Here it says that the departure of medical staff of Croatian ethnicity during the first half of 1993 was unjustified. This was produced by the Defence Department of Herceg-Bosna. Do you agree with that, sir, that it was unjustified?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I only agree that people left and that the hospital was in dire straits as regards staffing. As for the reasons of people leaving and my justifying or not a person's motives, I think everyone has to deal with that on their own, for themselves. A nurse who is not a soldier and has three children, if she decides to leave, I understand her decision. But as to whether it's justified, that's for somebody else to decide. I know that we were constantly short of staff, we were constantly trying to recruit more staff. And as for the conditions we worked in, there were weeks when people didn't leave their work posts. They worked to the point of exhaustion. And then there would be a lull in the war and after that they would come back to work and so on and so forth. So this was something that I hope will never happen anywhere again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Let's move to another subject related to the Health Sector. In the same document you will see, on page 26 and 27 and 28, there is a reference of all -- and this is in the B/C/S version, 29 and 30, of all the medical supplies and material value of goods and shipments that the hospital did receive, the war hospital in Mostar from the HVO, the health centre in Mostar, the medical supply service. I think the figures they speak for themselves. And you have a number -- under number 3, the origin of the donation throughout that time to the HVO Health Sector including your hospital and you also mentioned, we saw the video of donations from units from the UNPROFOR and here mentioning donations from UNHCR, Doctors Without Borders, and many international organisations to all the hospitals from the HVO throughout that time. Point 6, sir, of that report at the end says: "The work in the warehouse." And clearly says that the war conditions are quite bad because of unfavourable work temperature where all these medicines and supplies were stocked in Herceg-Bosna. And it says between brackets "favourable to the storage," and it says that "it's dusty and drafty due to large space, and on the other hand, we lack the space for receiving the goods and for permanent storage." So you have so much donations you lack for space to storage them. And in fact you have so much that you mention in your statement, sir, and here as well it's mentioned, that already in 1993 you have problems with medicines that were not used and then they need to be destroyed. And in this case, for example, you see that it mentions that in point 7, Dr. Ivo Curic, it mention in this report that around 100 tonnes of such material was destroyed under his supervision at that time. Do you agree with that, sir, with this report from the Health Sector?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I have to comment on it. I cannot agree a priori and I'll tell you why. All this is correct. For years throughout the war we received lots of donations from all over the world, enormous quantities of medicines and other material --

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: One second, sir. My question was -- I don't want you to comment. My question was whether you agree and you said that the information in this document was correct. That's what you said --

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: No, that is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Your Honour. I waited for the witness to answer. May the witness please be allowed to complete his answer. If not, then I will put the question to him in redirect but then it will be on my time. A question of ten lines has been put to him and he is not allowed to answer in two sentences. I think this is incorrect towards the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: At line 10, it says that all this is correct and he wanted to comment about the -- something else but I just want to ask -- I wanted to ask him whether he agree with that and he said all this is correct. Line 10 of the page we are discussing right now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not the way I said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also listen to what we said. If 100 tonnes of material is destroyed then there is a problem. Destroyed, is it done on purpose or is it because the products are past their shelf life? We have a doctor before us and he can maybe tell us why there is material that was actually destroyed. There is certainly a reason. Yes, doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the last comment about 100 tonnes destroyed is what I want to respond to. Let me repeat. We received a lot of that and I'm sure that these figures are taken from our books. But what I don't know or, rather, I don't know where this information comes from that 100 tonnes was destroyed because in Bosnia-Herzegovina we did not have facilities for destroying these quantities, for burning them. We don't have such an incinerator. We received a lot from Germany, and the media wrote about this for a long time, and I accept part of the problem was that the storage space was not appropriate. We had 3.000 square metres of an unfinished building and this could affect the quality of the medicines and their usability. I do have to give you an example which is something that rarely happens. There was a point in time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speak a little slowly, Mr. Witness, because in what you are saying the French interpreter is extraordinary, he manages to interpret what you are saying, but when I see in English there are things that are missing. You said awhile ago that you received from Germany solution dating back from 1950, and in the English text this is not mentioned. So kindly, kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I'll try. I have to complete my answer. At one point we had a situation where we had a mountain of medicines which had to be discarded, and we didn't know what to do with them so we took 200 barrels of 200 litres, put concrete inside and we stacked them all, and they were outside for a long time under a roof outside our hospital. This turned out to be an ecological problem and for years the press wrote about it. And to cut the story short we exported this medicine to be incinerated in Germany and we had to pay for this. We had to pay 150.000 German marks from the hospital funds for this to be destroyed. So Dr. Curic could not have incinerated this quantity of medicines. He may have incinerated other things but not medicines, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: This is a report from the Health Sector of the minister of defence and he says that the warehouse at the Heliodrom was used -- the warehouse at the Heliodrom was used to actually store the bulk of expired goods. That's on page 27 of the English version. Now --

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm speaking of the depot in the hospital in Bijeli Brijeg. I don't know about other warehouses. They did not come under my purview. I'm speaking of the depot in the hospital which was run by my pharmacists with some other people and then it came under the control of the health centre -- sector, but the location remained in the Bijeli Brijeg hospital until the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, I was a bit surprised when you talked about the solutions dating back from 1950 that the Germans sent to you. Does that mean there were donations of medicines that were already -- had already expired when they were sent to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not just the Germans, from all sorts of places. I don't want to lessen the value of the donations we received, because without these good quality donations, we could not have treated people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We didn't have money. But inside every truck-load there was always useless medicine and that ceased to surprise us after awhile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But a very ultra-technical question. Now, if a medicine has expired, take an antibiotic, for example, despite the fact that it has expired and that you have no medicines left, can you use this expired medicine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the medicine has been stored under good conditions. In the case of pills, for example, if the only problem is that the shelf life has expired, that it expired only a year ago, let's say, then you can use that because we know that this medicine is perhaps 20 or 30 per cent less effective so you just increase the dosage. So if you have nothing else to use, you can use those that appear to be in good conditions. But you cannot do this with syrups or capsules. You can do it with pills but you have to be cautious and only do this when you have no other option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for blood pouches, blood bags, are those that cannot be used once the date has expired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the case of blood there must be no deviation. Blood is an organ used under strictly controlled conditions, and it's better not to give it at all than if you are not doing it under proper conditions. In no case can you give a patient blood which is not in good order. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, you, yourself, you have given your Hippocratic oath; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: A long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And I understand clearly that you have done all the best to stick to it throughout the war and you treated any patient that came to your hands?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: But your actions did not reflect the policies of the HVO authorities because they didn't take any Hippocratic oath?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. [Overlapping speakers] I really don't want to object but this is unbelievable. I believe that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: It is believable. Let me continue with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, we can -- which is not allowed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, let the Prosecutor ask the questions and then the Judges will see whether -- if the question is so stupid then the Judges will draw the necessary consequences. Very well, Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know what you wanted to demonstrate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The President's microphone has gone off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Forgive me, Mr. Prosecutor, my microphone was not working. I don't know what you wanted to demonstrate. It raised an objection from Mr. Kovacic. I wanted to say that if the question is a stupid one, then the Judges will draw the necessary consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. What I wanted to point out here is the fact that we have heard throughout the testimony of the witness that, of course, him, himself, as a doctor, and I agree completely with the witness, he has treated any patient irrespective of whether they were either Muslims or Croats or whatever nationality, or whether he was a soldier or -- meaning a combatant or a non-combatant. He and his staff under his command, they treat everyone. But -- and he also mentioned that he never dismiss anyone from his job because they left there, the position at work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And that is my point. The reality is, sir, that many of your medical staff, you didn't dismiss them but, for example, after the 9 of May, most of your Bosnian Muslim staff were arrested, and their families as well, and they were taken to the Heliodrom; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Objection. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, the Prosecutor has the right to ask this question because for the Prosecutor, he believes that after the 9th of May there were arrests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just small -- there is presumption in the question. That means the Prosecutor first have to establish whether this presumption is correct; or in other words, whether the witness knows about that and then put the question. This is it. If I'm wrong, I'm wrong. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, try and check first that the witness is actually aware. You went straight to the heart of the problem. Some rather that there be preliminary steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember saying to counsel that in May 1993 your personnel Bosnian Muslim were rounded up and taken to the Heliodrom? Do you remember some of the doctors working for you, Bosnian Muslim, were rounded up and taken to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I remember very well what I said --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question does not -- was not raised in cross-examination. The Prosecutor in -- so this was not raised in the examination-in-chief. The Prosecutor is again mixing up the statement given to Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Ms. Nozica. The problem is that there is a document that the Prosecutor will undoubtedly quote, P 2037, where in this document the doctor is going to intervene to free somebody. That is the whole problem. So let the Prosecutor carry out his cross-examination. It is important to know why an anaesthesiologist was actually arrested and why he intervenes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just add something. This comes up almost every time there is a cross-examination, and it is quite clear that cross-examination is not limited to the subject matters of the direct if there are questions put that may assist the case of the party which does the cross-examination. We have applied it like this when the Defence cross-examined and we have applied it consistently now where it is the Prosecutor that cross-examines. And I -- I find it a bit surprising that we have to repeat it practically every week.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, excuse me, please, by your leave, I have to say this. On page 55, in line 6, it says here that, to the question of the counsel, he said that Bosnian Muslims went to Heliodrom. I intervened because I did not put questions about that. I know that the witness can be questioned as to his credibility, he can be impeached on any topic but I just wanted to say that I did not put this question during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree. The document as at P 02367. Mr. Prosecutor, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: You mentioned that all employees, you treated all employees equally. Only you. Now, sir, let me show you a short video of what happened the 9th of May. And that's P 04238, Prosecution Exhibit P 0215 -- please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] This shows a picture of ethnic cleansing this time carried out by the Croats. According to UN observers, they lack food and blankets. They have been rounded up by force so that they could take nothing with them. There are many families deliberately separated." "Journalist: [Previous translation continues] ... work out how to deal with the hundreds of Muslims they evicted from their homes in Mostar when the fighting began last Sunday. They deny this is some kind of ethnic cleansing. 1400 detainees are being held at an old barracks on the edge of the airport. We were allowed to show them but not the building which looks like a prison. The Croats know the power of an image." "Unidentified speaker: We'll be forced to move these people, said their commander, to somewhere less safe, that doesn't look like a prison. The detainees themselves have been correctly treated, but are not here by choice." "Unidentified speaker: They tell us we must go with them and we must go, but we crying and we don't want to go with them." "Journalist: Under present plans, the detainees will be returned in the next day or two to seek parts of the city. The problem is, there aren't any safe parts of the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, now, with this introduction, this video, to refresh your recollection what was going on on the 9th of May with some -- or the Bosnian Muslim population as being reported by -- internationally, I want you to concentrate on Exhibit P 02315. And do you have it with you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Please, if the Registrar can assist me. Exhibit P 02315. 02315. Maybe it's there behind you. Is it there behind you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, if you can see it's on the e-court, the document. My apologies for that. At the end of the page of -- this is a report. It's a list of medical staff, employees, sorry, of the Mostar HVO regional field hospital and their family members who were taken away from their flats. Right, you see that, sir? You have it now with you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Right. At the end of this document, sir, there is a signature of the commander of the regional field hospital. Is that your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: No, this is the signature of Dr. Ante Kresic, my assistant, a pediatrician from Mostar. Of course I know about this list. When wartime events started that morning, we had chaos. A great many wounded. The situation was truly chaotic. And in all that upheaval, people came to report to me that some people had not reported to work because they had been taken to a place near Mostar. I called Dr. Ante Kresic, my assistant who was in charge of the health centre which was part of the regional hospital in organisational terms, and I told him to make a list of all the people who had not reported to work that morning in every ward. In the meantime, Dr. Erac [phoen], my assistant for surgery and surgical branches, came to tell me that people had also failed to show up for work there. And when Dr. Ante Kresic drew up the list, I responded by asking that these people be sent back. And within a few hours, Dr. Rebac and the engineer Cujic brought some people back by car, and within the space of two days, they all returned to work and many of them are still working there today. You said that they had been imprisoned; I don't know whether they had been imprisoned or not. I know that they had not come to work. I was at the hospital at the time, struggling to deal with the situation, and all these people came back to work ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, here it says list of employees of the Mostar regional field office hospital and their family members who were taken away from their flats. Did you order, sir, as a commander of the hospital that your employees, these were employees under your command, were taken out of the hospital on the 9 of May? Were you the one that ordered this? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I absolutely reject this. I definitely did not. I only asked that they be sent back and that's what happened. Never in my life do I punish people. I don't punish my family members, let alone people at work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir. Do you know who ordered them to be taken out of their flats. You saw the girl saying that she didn't want to get out from the flats --

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I really don't know that. All I know is that on that day it was a disaster. And speaking as a human being, it seems more logical that they were taken to be kept safe and not to die in the streets, but that is my own interpretation. That's how I see it. It was all very sad and very difficult but we came through it in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm rather troubled by the title of this document. You said that your deputy was the one to have drafted and signed this document. That's fine. But why does it carry this title? That's what I don't understand. The fact that people working at the hospital were taken to the Heliodrom, that's one thing, but why do we have this title here? You and your colleague, you knew that they had left their apartments, their flats or that they had been taken away from their flats. Could you read in your own language because I'm always wary of the English translations, could you tell me in your own language, could you read to me the title of this document? It begins with "Spisak." Could you read that out to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. "List of employees of the regional war hospital of the Mostar HVO and members of their families who were taken away from their flats." May I comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The list was drawn up by my assistant. The list is correct. It shows that people left and came back. Why did this happen? I don't know if any of you have ever been in a city or a town where so many projectiles land in such a short space of time. People were fleeing from their flats trying to find shelter. At that point somebody rounded them up into trucks and take them away -- took them away from the burning town which was all in flames and smoke. So I think it was much better for them to be taken away and to stay alive, and you can call it what you like, then they that they die in the streets and that we later be declared criminals who killed them in the streets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Prosecutor, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, let's see what happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Prosecutor. I would like to ask a question of you with regard to your last statement. Wasn't it a terrible discrimination that all the poor Croats in Mostar were left in hell and only the Muslims were saved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this same list there are people who are not Muslims, for example, for example, Ivan Marinovic. Then there are others. Savo Popovic is not a Muslim. Jasna Culjak is not a Muslim. Miletic Edin, he is not a Muslim either. I know him personally. His name looks Muslim but he is not. And, well, I won't look any further, but Ranko Milicevic, likewise, is not a Muslim. People were going to work and this happened. This started happening at 7.00. Since I started from Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: In the same list you have the name of Ahmed Mujic. Number 9 listed. Do you remember what happened with Mr. Ahmed -- Dr. Ahmed Mujic, later on, in October 1993? Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Let's see Exhibit P 05944.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It does not figure in our --

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sorry. My apologies. P 05939.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: So you see it now? Okay. So that's it. Perfect. Just keep that document in ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to get the record right because the number you have indicated does not figure now. Was it P 05939?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: 5939. That's it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: I made a mistake myself, and I apologise to the Registry. I mentioned two exhibits. The one which is being shown now to the witness is P 05944. And the following document that I will show to you after this one is P 05939, as Your Honour mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: So in this first one, sir, you can see that there is a protest there and --

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, but the father of Dr. Travljanin, I've never seen him, but I know his daughter and I know of the whole case. And he was born in 1914.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Let me ask you the question, sir. This is a protest written on 18 October 1993, addressed to Mr. Bruno Stojic, signed by Dr. Ante Kvesic, you, and Brigadier Dr. Ivan Bagaric. Do you recognise your signature there, sir, in this document?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Let's read the protest: "In early morning hours of 18 October 1993, Dr. Slavenka Travljanin and her father were killed in their apartment by unknown persons. Civilians and in uniform -- and uniform, while the mother was wounded. Dr. Slavenka Travljanin spent the entire war working for the dialysis centre of the HVO Mostar regional hospital," you mentioned that you were in the dire need of dialysis people. "As neurology subspecialist, she set an example to others in her work and relations with colleagues and patients." Now, a little bit farther in this protest that you signed, sir, and you addressed to Mr. Stojic in October 1993, it says further on that: "These were loyal workers of the HVO Mostar and this tragic and shameful example we warn you for the last time that we were not able to restrain either the Muslims or Croatian medical staff in the RRB HVO Mostar because of this. The workers of both the Health Sector and the RRB HVO Mostar are disgusted by this type of terror inflicted on their colleagues in the town which is not the first of this kind. It's not the first of its kind. This is why we urgently ask the concrete measures to be undertaken." I have only one question on this, sir. Were they Bosnian Muslim, these doctors?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: These are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: My second question, sir. In this report do you recognise, as you sit here, that this was not the first kind of terror inflicted to your colleagues? We are talking about October 1993. Do agree with what you have written at that time, sir; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: In principle I never give yes or no answers but I can explain and go back to your first question. There is no yes or no answer as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Did you write this protest, sir, yes or no? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: But your first question wasn't that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, going back to the document we were discussing, P 02315, and in the same list under internal medicine guard you have - one second - 21, Nevzeta Kreso. And I will ask, please, to be shown also in e-court Exhibit P 03219. P 03219. This is a request, sir, it's not done by you, it's a request dated 6 July 1993, and it reflects, sir, a request of the Convicts Battalion from the HVO, asking to release the family of Dr. Kreso parents from the facility. And they say that: "We need that in order to manipulate with other Muslims in Bijelo Polje, and they will be returned." Returned to the prison, I take it. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: But I don't know what you want to say by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Did you know, sir, that staff under your command, did you know that the family of Dr. Kreso were arrested? Did you know that? That in July 1993 they were arrested? ? You didn't know? Please, we need an audible answer?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: How should I know? Well, I'm not an idiot that I can pull this way and that. I made a list of people who did not come to work on the 9th of May. After that, I didn't investigate. I was in hospital -- in the hospital doing my work. I don't know what happened in any other sphere. I was on call in the hospital 24 hours, and I said that Dr. Kreso was not from my hospital. Some people left and returned. I don't even know the man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, please remain calm. Nobody is trying to manipulate you. You are a witness for justice since you are under oath and the question that anyone might ask is when you have a colleague who disappears because he has been arrested, you might wonder what you do to find out what happened to him. If I tomorrow, for instance, or I see Judge Prandler disappearing tomorrow, I shall wonder where he has gone, what's happened to him. You see what I mean? This is a question I ask you. Amongst your colleagues some were, let's say, arrested. Now, the question is what do you do to find out why were they arrested; and two, what you do so that they can come back as quickly as possible to do their medical work. That's the underlying question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to that question, my answer will be the same as the first time. When it concerned the hospital staff, I did everything necessary, everything that was possible and all the people returned to work. I'm sorry that the Prosecutor didn't give me an opportunity to explain the situation around Dr. Travljanin because that is indeed something that needs to be clarified. And when it comes to Dr. Kreso, I don't know the man. He wasn't in my hospital and I've never seen him. So I can't look for somebody in Holland, for example, who has gone missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Just for the record that Dr. Nevzeta Kreso was in the hospital and he is listed under internal medicine, ward number 21. My following exhibit excerpts for you is Exhibit P 02367.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] ... the Prosecutor was witnessing, I would advise him to read this document until the last line. In the last line it said -- it connected this person with Bijelo Polje; that is a third location. That has nothing to do. So the witness here said, I don't know this Dr. Kreso, and the Prosecutor now knows that this is the same Dr. Kreso who worked in the hospital. Kreso is a frequent name. Stand up and tell them. Kreso is a very common name. We don't know here whether it is male or female, whether it is the same Kreso or any other, but if the Prosecutor know, he can testify no problem. I think this is a really far-reaching conclusion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, Dr. Kreso, this Dr. Kreso was he was one working under number 21 as an internal medical doctor? Is he the same one as the one that we talked about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I leave that assessment to the Trial Chamber, sir. And I will continue with the following exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the Prosecutor should make a choice. Either he is testifying or should he ask you to make a conclusion without the facts. We are here to establish the facts and then the honourable Chamber will draw up conclusions, but facts the parties are here for. So is it a fact or not. Maybe the witness may help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this person called Kreso, was he arrested or did he continue working with you in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat, on the first list all those people returned. After that, Dr. Kreso left the internal medicine department and I never saw her again. And her husband, I know he is a doctor, too, but I've never seen him. So I have absolutely no knowledge that in July -- now, listen, the list I was commenting on was the 9th of May, and they were taken away and returned. But what happened to this lady doctor in July and she was no longer in my hospital, I mean, the hospital on the west bank, I really can't say. And I don't know that all the staff in my hospital. It's impossible; there are too many of them. But I'm certain that she was no longer in the hospital so that's what I can say. So you are referring to a different situation now and a different month. It's July. So please don't mix up apples and pears. I have a list and I stand by that list, and then I've been given an exhibit here that I know nothing about and isn't my document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, on the list on the letter in P 023 -- 03219 that we have here, in the B/C/S version reference is made to Doktora Kreso. Am I right in assuming that this is female?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally don't know if it's a man or a woman because they were a married couple of doctors, both the wife and the husband were doctors. But in the internal medicine department was a lady doctor but I didn't meet her ever either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kvesic, naively and not being conversant with the Croat language, I would have assumed that it makes a difference between Doktor, and that would be male, and Doktora, and that would be female; is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, grammatically correct but what usually happens in lists you have the DR, and that's for doctor, so you can conclude what you like. I can't say either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, here for once we do not have an abbreviation. Do you know several female doctors by the name of Kreso?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally don't know this one either. This lady either. All I know is that she was in the internal medicine department. And let me tell you that I was commander for a very short time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, let's go to Exhibit P 02367. That exhibit, sir, is dated 13 May 1993, and we already discussed in the document from the health department from the minister of -- from the Defence of the HVO which says that there was a especially a lack of surgeons and anaesthesiologists in the hospital throughout that period in 1993. And if you see this request, sir, this request says commander of the Mostar Croatian Defence Council war hospital, Dr. Ante Kvesic, is the signature. Is this yours, sir? That's your document?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: I'm going to read the document, sir. And it says: "Request: We ask you to release the family (two children and parents) of Dr. Emir or Emira Bebanic who is working as an anaesthesiologist at the Mostar Croatian Defence Council Regional War Hospital for five days without a break." And then, "Driver Hajrudin Begic drives to most dangerous places ever since the war started, so we ask you to provide his family the opportunity to go home, including Safet, Mejra and Zejna Hadzic. Surgeon Dr. Drace works places ever since the war started, and so we ask you to release his family, including his mother Emina Drace, his brother Nedzad and his sister-in-law Sanja." Sir, they have to release the first anaesthesiologist at least for five days without a break, to be released from where? Do you remember, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Of course I remember but could you please state the context of the first sentence exactly. I ask that Dr. Emira Bebanic work for five days in surgery continuously and I requested that she be released. So she wasn't in Heliodrom for five days; she was in the hospital throughout. But I used my authority to help these people meet up with their family members and I'm very proud of that. I did that in several instances so I see nothing wrong there. I think that's what I should have done. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: I agree with you. My question is -- don't take it personally. My question is -- I'm asking you only, you said that they have to be released. From where they have to be released, these people?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: People came to me working in the hospital and complained that when these people were rounded up in town, that parts of their families had been taken away, I mean to Heliodrom, but I'm not sure. And so I wrote this request, loud and clear, and signed it and they took the request with them and took them to the various administrative bodies. I don't know where; I didn't take the request. But they obviously did take copies and obviously they were successful because they didn't come back with the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to imagine what your position is. It's difficult but Judges must try to understand things. You at the time were in charge of that hospital, the so-called wartime hospital. Now, a colleague of yours Dr. Bebanic, who apparently works very hard as an anaesthesiologist since you state that he worked five days without interruption. If he -- since he was the only anaesthesiologist. So five days, five days, he must have been very tired indeed. Dr. Bebanic must say to you in that case, well, Look my family has been arrested, my children and my parents both. That's an important thing he is saying to you. You draft this document. Now, nobody complains about that. But when he says to you that his children have been arrested, you must wonder about why have the children of this doctor been arrested. Did you call somebody on the phone, for instance, at the Department of Defence to ask for explanations? What did it mean that children were arrested, children of a doctor who was working at the military hospital of the HVO? Did you do that or did you simply do the minimum service, i.e., give in a written request to -- actually we don't know to whom, so that these people should be released? Do you remember the context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During those days and the situations that occurred, I'll remember for as long as I live, you can't forget things like that. I was just 29 when I became commander of the hospital and I think this is something that you have during your upbringing. I wanted to stay on on the hospital as a doctor and as a human being. That was my ambition. And you saw a moment ago that I succeeded in that because as a human being, I'm very proud when I walk the streets of Mostar and I never fail to help people. And I said at the outset, and I didn't want somebody -- don't want somebody to misunderstand this but I personally used my car, for example, to transport people. Nothing was too much for me if I could help people. So you can ask the people, the locals what the commander of the war hospital was like. I'm really proud of my work there and I never failed to help a fellow human being. Now, specifically whether I drove the doctor or not, possibly I did, but I can't claim that I did. It was in 1993, after all, so I've forgotten. A lot of time has gone by and sometimes I do my best to forget because they were very difficult timed and a burden if you kept thinking about them. So let me repeat: I'm very proud of everything I did, as a human being and as a doctor in the hospital and there's nobody in this world whom I would not talk to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You aren't answering my question. You are the commander of the military hospital, a colleague who is Dr. Bebanic, tells you, My children and my parents have been arrested. At that time I want to know whether you telephoned your authorities to signal the problem, or you simply did the minimum, namely the document that we have before us? Because you see, for me, tomorrow if my colleague tells me his children have been arrested, I don't think I'll just, you know, pay a minimum service. I will try to find out why my colleague's children have been arrested. In particular, if I exercise a function of authority. That's what I'm trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me repeat. As commander of the hospital, I reacted in every situation to the full as a human being, that is my constitutional makeup and I propose that you ring up Dr. Bebanic, the lady doctor, and I'm sure she'll be able to give you a much better answer. I never omitted to do something to help. Now, you refer to these children who were arrested and I state that those children were taken away to safety because it was terrible in those streets and we didn't have anywhere else to put those children up. We didn't have any nursery schools or anything like that. So I allow for the possibility that some people, in their own minds, would invert things but those children were not mistreated, they were not prisoners, they were just taken out of a town that was burning. And I suggest that you call this lady doctor, Dr. Bebanic, and ask her to tell you how things stood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, you are not a legal expert, we know that you are 29 years old, we can understand that. But in your document you talk about released. And if you say released, that means they had been these people had been arrested. You see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we could discuss linguistics here. If somebody has been taken to an area that is protected and then released from that area, doesn't mean necessarily that they were in prison. I'm not a lawyer and I don't think I would be a lawyer in a second life, but I will not allow somebody to comment my acts and to reverse them. Let me repeat. At all times I did everything I could within my power to help people and even sometimes surpassed what was called for. It was never a problem for me to get into my car and drive somebody where they needed to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a clarification on the document that we have, what I don't seem to be able to see who is this document addressed to? This protest letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see in the heading, it was sent to the Defence Department, and Dr. Bagaric always reacted the same way as I did. Our reactions were always geared towards helping people. And now 15 and 16 years on, I don't know who this was addressed to because I haven't seen this document for 16 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is addressed to the Department of Defence because in actual fact the authority to which you have sent this letter of protest could be in a measure not only to release the persons if it had the authority, but also to explain the reasons for which these persons were retained or arrested or displaced, depending on the term that you prefer to use. But then you say that after so many years you don't remember which persons -- which authorities you had addressed yourself to; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know -- well, it's been 16 years since that time but I remember when the lady doctor arrived, I remember that we wrote this document, I remember that my driver drove her. But this is 16 years on. If I had to take an oath, I'd have to stop and think because 16 years is a long period of time, especially if one wishes to forget certain events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Prosecutor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Let's continue with Exhibit P 03064.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll break in a few minutes. The interpretation didn't function. I was saying that we'll have to take a break in a few minutes. Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: 03064. Otherwise it's on e-court, you can see it on your display on the computer. Thank you very much, usher. And this is an order, 1st July, 1993, so almost a month after the 9 of May, 1993, and it's an order. And let me read for you, sir: "Order: Based on the request by Mr. Ante Kvesic, commander of the regional war hospital in Mostar, and in order to provide necessary anaesthesia and blood transfusion, the following persons are to be transported to Zeljko Coric, communications officer of the HVO main medical staff, who will take them to their work-place." Number 1, Mujo Duric; second, Zlatko Kazazic; three, Zlatko Taslaman. Authorised and approved by Mr. Berislav Pusic. And we remember, sir, that you said, and it was mentioned in the report, that there were a need of anaesthesiologists earlier. Where were these people, sir? Where they were have to be taken from?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: These were employees of my hospital and I ask that they be returned because obviously they were at Heliodrom. But I'd just like to repeat, you said one month later. I don't know when they were taken; they weren't taken during the first days but sometime later on. Now, whenever information reached me that a staff member had been taken away somewhere always reacted and asked that they be returned. Always and in all situations and quite obviously in this one too. So I don't know who I sent this request to. I can't remember everything. I mean, my hardware is set up differently. I would like you to find my request so that we could comment on that and not this. I'm sure I have it somewhere in my hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, I would also like to but, unfortunately, I don't have it here today. The important thing here, sir, is that upon your request it was ordered a release of these people in July that were at the Heliodrom and that they went to work to provide the necessary anaesthesia and blood transfusion?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. I requested that they be released, so the order was issued by someone else to someone else. I requested. That's what it says. An order and a request are not the same, in Croatian at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Do you remember why they were arrested, these people, sir, and sent to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I have absolutely no idea. I went into action when I found that they were not at work and I requested that they be returned and they were, but I didn't conduct any investigations. How should I know why somebody was considered a suspect or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that only the needed medical staff, the indispensable medical staff who were Bosnian Muslim and who were arrested at the Heliodrom were the only ones that, upon your request, were released to work in your hospital because of a lack of an anaesthesiologist or the lack of surgeons or the lack of other medical staff?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Incorrect. I asked for all those who were absent. And let me repeat that. And on the first list we saw not everybody was Bosniak, so I -- whenever I received information that some people were missing, I requested that they be returned. All of them. And I'd like you to bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: I have one more document before the break, Your Honours, if you allow me. P 02377.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And, sir, this is another -- it's a list of personnel of the service for engineering and maintenance of facilities whose work is indispensable for the Croatian Defence Council in Mostar regional war hospital. And you have the names of the people there, Emir Dizdarevic, Elvir Selimotic, Sule Drljevic not there. Apparently it wasn't there. Mirsad Grebovic and Dzemal Behram and it's signed by Dr. Ante Kvesic. So these people were really indispensable for the work of the hospital; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Of course, because a hospital doesn't mean anaesthesia alone. You had to have maintenance of the facilities and everything else. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I have to react for the benefit of everyone in the courtroom because the translation of the stamp under Dr. Kvesic's name is wrong. On the original stamp it says the Republic of Bosnian Herzegovina, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mostar, regional war hospital, Health Sector, Defence Department. Whereas in the English version, the English translation, it says that it is a stamp of the military police administration. I'm referring to the upper stamp and I think this is an important point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, again we have seen a list of people, they were either surgeons, anaesthesiologists, blood transfusions and engineers which were indispensable to the work of the HVO hospital. Isn't it true, sir, that the Bosnian Muslim medical staff that were released from the Heliodrom were released because they were indispensable for the work of the HVO hospital?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Absolutely incorrect. Now, I can remember, for example, for gynaecology, you have the same surname for seven people, a whole family, just not the lady doctor who was on the job and hadn't been taken away. So I asked in the same way for everybody to be returned. I wasn't interested in anything else. And if you look at gynaecology on the first list, it's just the lady doctor that was there. But as I said, the important thing was that when I saw that somebody was missing, I reacted and asked that they be returned. I took steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll going to take a break. You have 10 minutes, Mr. Prosecutor. See how you get organised so you can actually deal with the documents that you haven't dealt with up until now. We'll be resuming in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, as I said to you, you have 10 minutes remaining, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, Dr. Kvesic, I want you to go back to a document that was discussed with counsel in the beginning of your testimony, 2D 00566. And do you have it with you, sir, do you have it in front of you, the document?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: This is a list of wounded members of the ABiH, as it's said there, who were sent from the HVO war hospital in Mostar to Split. And you were saying in the beginning of your testimony today that some of them, they seemed that were from the ABiH, some of them it doesn't say whether they were from the ABiH, but they were transferred to Split from Mostar west hospital for further treatment. I want you to -- to ask you, do you know the circumstances, for example, in which Saric Senad, which is number 5 in that list, was wounded? Do you remember, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I can only tell how serious the injuries were by the diagnosis, but I cannot say anything about the circumstances of injury. The reason these people were transferred was that these injuries were extremely serious. So we were unable to deal with them properly. If you see that this man has a fractured back bone, that's very serious and our surgeons couldn't deal with it. And if a man is a paraplegic because of an injury to the spinal cord, these are very serious injuries. So we just gave them first aid, primary treatment to save their lives but then we had to send them on to receive proper treatment. Some were -- and some were not. Some have been entered as members of the ABiH and others were members but nobody wrote this down. It didn't matter. They were seriously wounded so they had to be transported to Split in order to get proper treatment, the kind of treatment they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I will ask you just to keep that document with you. I will ask you to keep that document with you, and then to focus in the following one, which is related to this document. And this is Exhibit from the Prosecution, P 03936. You can see it, I'm sure, in electronic format. P 03936. And this -- do you have it with you, the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: This report from the 4 August 1993, we see that on the 5th of August, the person -- this person Senad Saric was transferred. So this document is from one day before, the 4 of August. It says that the detainee Senad Saric was wounded when they were working for one of -- for the light assault brigade. Do you see that, sir? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes, but what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: My question is to see that this person that you mentioned here, Senad Saric, the circumstances under which he was wounded?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: As to the circumstances, I don't know about them. We received the patient, admitted him to hospital, and did whatever we could for him. But truly, I cannot comment on the circumstances. I can speculate or not, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: All right. Sir, and we still have this document, 2D 00566. For example, let's see another patient was a Muslim that was transferred on the 15 August 1993. And Kadus Anija [phoen], he was transferred on the 15 of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And I will ask the Registry to show to the witness document P 04157.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Now, this document is also dated 13 August 1993. The person was transferred on the 15 August 1993 for further treatment. Here it says that Nijaz Kladusak was wounded by the BH Army and was kept for treatment. Let's continue with another document related to that list. Number 10 in the list of people that you certified that were severely wounded and transferred to Split. Kurtovic Mirsad, that's Exhibit P 04668 from the Prosecution. P 04668. Again this document is 31 August 1993. And then on the 2nd September, 1993, Mr. Mirsad Kurtovic was transferred to Split and in the report from the general present for Mr. Stanko Bozic says that he was wounded by the sniper enemy where he working as a detainee. This was a detainee from earlier on. My question, sir, to you is: Do you remember whether many people or some Bosnian Muslims as these ones that were transferred for treatment at your hospital were Bosnian Muslims that were detainees at the Heliodrom, the ones that were transferred with these severe and serious injuries?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: I keep repeating two things. I was the commander of the hospital. Whoever needed hospital treatment came to the hospital and they were always taken care of. Outside the hospital, I really don't know. I really don't know how these people were wounded or where. My job was not to find that out because I was not in the police force. Either one or the other. I was a doctor trying to keep the hospital well supplied, to keep it running and we never omitted do whatever we could for a patient. So I really don't know anything about this. I did not participate in that. From the moment the patient arrived in hospital to the time he was transferred to Split, that's what I know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's concentrate now on Exhibit P 05465.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you are saying but let's take the example of a person that you may have operated. Normally the doctors would go and see him, discuss with him, to ask what his state is like, whether he is getting better, does he have running a fever, and as in your profession as a doctor that's a psychological dimension as well, you have to talk to the patient. The patient is not an object. So somebody who is wounded by a sniper and who is hospitalised and operated, he will say yes, I received a bullet, I don't know where it came from, and at that time the physician will talk to the patient. Is that not how it happened in your hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely agree that a patient needs to be psychologically uplifted, but he will certainly not be uplifted by talking about snipers and how he was wounded. You have to give him back his will to live, not try to knock it out of him. Because everybody in wartime was hit by shrapnel or bullets or whatever, so I absolutely distance myself from things that happened where I was not present and didn't see what was going on. I really did nothing outside the hospital and I really don't see how I can answer questions about things I wasn't part of. I really don't know. I'm telling you, I don't know. I'm willing to tell you everything I know. I know all about the hospital and I'll tell you all about that. As for the rest, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you don't know, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a collateral question, Mr. Kvesic. These patients, would you personally have seen them, all or some, or would they have been -- I mean, you were, after all, the commander of the hospital and had enormous administrative tasks. To what extent were you involved in the immediate medical activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hospital has two segments of work. One is to make sure it has the necessary equipment and supplies. And the other part is that you have professional staff who know their jobs. So I was not dealing directly with patients. I was dealing with the logistics, trying to ensure food for the patients and the staff through donations and by other means. We also had problems with fuel, with tyres for our vehicles, with money. So I was struggling to keep the hospital afloat. Others were working directly with the patients. As I'm quite a lively person by nature, I did visit the patients because I was interested in them. But I did not work with them as a doctor until 1994, when I devoted myself to pediatric surgery, and since then, of course, I have been working with patients and I still do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, your time has practically expired. You can ask one last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, let's focus on Exhibit P 05465. 05465. This is a letter sent from the warden of the Heliodrom Stanko Bosic to your superior Brigadier Ivan Bagaric. And if you see from 29 September 1993, sir, and it concerns the work at your hospital because your work will be affected by this one. And it says that it's informing about the difficulties and problems encountered regarding the treatment of some severely wounded and sick inmates due to inadequate accommodation and insufficient material and medicaments at the Heliodrom. And he's asking -- asking Dr. Bagaric to transfer the sick persons mentioned above and enable them to be treated in the hospital due to the forthcoming visit of International Red Cross committee; otherwise they will -- and in order to prevent them for finding the sick in an inappropriate condition and treatment conditions and consequently getting an unfavourable impression of the centre and military prison, which would be detrimental for the HVO. So, my question is: Sir, did you know that Muslim patients that you were treating were wounded during forced labour or at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: For the fifth time, you are trying to put a question to me about something I don't know. I know that whenever anyone had to bring a patient to hospital, they were able to do that from anywhere. But I don't know about these circumstances. I never visited the Heliodrom in my life, before or during or after the war. I have never been there. I was in the hospital and I barely had time to deal with matters at the hospital. I didn't have time to go home and see my children, let alone look in on other people's business. I don't know what other people were doing especially if their work had nothing to do with me. My work started when the patient arrived at the hospital door. It was a hospital and that's the way it operated. We never omitted to respond. There were difficult days, that's true. We had to bury our doctors, our technicians who got killed. That was life. At the hospital we had 6 or 7.000 wounded, can you imagine that number, in circumstances where the building was damaged, where we were short of staff, and you keep asking me about a place I've never been to. You keep asking me questions about things I don't know anything about. I'm sorry, but I have to tell you that because I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, your time is up. Witness, a sequel question as it were, this shouldn't raise any problem with you. In this hospital which was filled with patients, well, the international organisation such as the Red Cross or others, did they come and see the patients whatever their origin, Croats, Muslim, Serbs, did they come and visit them, were they allowed to enter freely in the hospital? And did they have confidential conversations with the patient, these representatives of these international organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they did. They could do whatever they liked. There was no porter at the door. The door was wide open. And apart from them who often came, journalists also walked in. There are thousands and thousands of metres of videotape filmed by various TV crews. We had nothing to hide and we never tried to hide anything. I'm proud of what the hospital did in the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, so if I have understood you properly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely wide open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So there were no guards preventing people from entering, anybody could go into the hospital and see who they wished, as long as they abided by visiting hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, anyone could enter our hospital at any time, except at night when the patients were asleep. When they came to see the patients, they would bring them something. The hospital was operating under terrible conditions and, of course, people were surprised at the conditions we were working in. Whoever wanted to visit the hospital to visit the patients could always do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Nozica, do you have any redirect questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly. I know this is being taken from my time and I will be really brief with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kvesic, I will put the document in e-court. It's P 05939. Let me remind you, that's the protest you signed, as did Mr. Bagaric, and it had to do with your lady doctor, Slavenka Travljanin, and her father. You have the document on the screen. Tell me briefly, was whatever had to be done pursuant to your protest actually done and do you have any knowledge that -- are you aware that an investigation was started?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: When the tragedy of Dr. Travljanin happened -- and I'm sorry when the Prosecutor asked me about her father whom I had never seen and I said I didn't know him, that was her father, but this was one of the worst days we had in the hospital, she was a wonderful person. The patients at the dialysis simply adored her because she was such a wonderful woman. When she was killed, the medical staff, Dr. Bagaric, the hospital, we did everything we could, not only by this protest but by petitions we signed. And the Minister of Defence, Bruno Stojic, organised an urgent meeting of all ministers and everyone insisted that an investigation be instituted to find the doctor's murderer. I know that an investigation was instigated. I don't know whether her murderer was ever found or not; I didn't have access to this information. We really did everything that we could. That was a time of fierce conflict and for the first time in my life I visited the Muslim cemetery. I held a speech at the funeral for the lady doctor. This was very hard for me to do, but she was such a wonderful woman. And because of our respect for her and because we didn't want this ever to happen again to anyone, we responded in whatever we knew how, through petitions, protests, in every way, and the minister of defence organised an urgent meeting. I remember that meeting, where the minister of the MUP and the military police were asked to do whatever they could to find the murderer and they started an investigation but whether it was ever completed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, let's dwell a little longer on this document and I'll tell you why. There was a document which was identical to this one. It had the same heading, Defence Department health centre, and it had the same number. I won't call it up on e-court yet. I will later. P 02367. When His Honour Judge Mindua asked you, you said it was a document sent to the Defence Department but does it say in this document Defence Department Health Sector, and its actually addressed to Mr. Stojic. So does the heading mean that this is where the document was sent from? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, we will look at what happened with the investigation. You have the document in the Prosecution binder, but it might be faster if we just look at it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at P 7035. Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the Prosecution binder you have this document. This is an exhibit, and it's information about crimes in the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have in e-court page 12 in English, and ERN 0102-9700 in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, please look at the note under the date of the 18th of October. It says here on the 18th of October, 19 -- or, rather, yes. In Mahe Djikica Street, Ahmed Mujic and his daughter, Slavenka Mujic Travljanin, were killed. The identity of the perpetrator is unknown and an investigation has begun. Is that this investigation?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's now go back to the document His Honour Judge Mindua asked you about, and that's P 2367. Yes, that's the document. His Honour Judge Mindua asked you to whom this document was addressed and transcript page 72, line 3, you said the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the document be scrolled down a little bit, please. Or rather, yes -- could we look at the upper part. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It says here Defence Department Health Sector, and we see the same number. Mr. Kvesic, was this sent from the Health Sector or is it sent to the Health Sector of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: It's from the Health Sector. Well, when it comes to administrative and legal matters, I find it hard to find my way around, and it's very easy for me to become confused in this respect. The Health Sector was part of the Defence Department and we sent this letter to the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Kvesic, the Prosecutor asked you about the Hippocratic oath. Could you please tell Their Honours whether any of the accused in this case, you see three of them here, and I will tell you that Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Prlic, and Mr. Coric who are not present are also accused. Mr. Praljak, Mr. Pusic, Mr. Stojic are here, have any of them ever complained to you or have they told you not to work in the way you did? If you had any contact with them, did they support you in your work at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Nozica. To which question of cross-examination does this relate? Because you are limited in redirect to points raised in the cross-examination and it appears to me that this does not figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will just remind you, the Prosecutor said, You took a Hippocratic oath, but what about the policy conducted by the others. I remember that the word "policy" was used. I am not wrong, Your Honours. I'm quite sure about this. If a reference is needed, I will tell you the page number, but my colleagues are indicating that I'm not wrong and the witness knows what I'm asking him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you answer, witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The Prosecutor was actually stopped before he had even finish the sentence. But I take your explanation and go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It's quite significant, in my view, that the question is recorded in the transcript. That's why I want the witness to explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctors always take the Hippocratic oath in a solemn manner, and throughout their professional lives they abide by that oath. In the hospital in wartime, nobody ever brought us into a situation where we were told to do our job like this or like that. In all logistical matters whenever we asked for assistance from any of these people, we received it, we received their support, and we were always commended for the work of the medical corps and the hospital and I think we deserved that. On all sides, the medical corps rose to the task during this war.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kvesic, when you say these people, are you referring to the people I enumerated because I did that on purpose?

utterances.speaker: ANTE KVESIC
utterances.text: In view of the post they had, the minister of defence made it possible to use the logistics from Grude for the hospital while we were able to obtain fuel, tyres, food and so on, especially at a time when they had consolidated themselves and had this material available. The hospital was given full support and a green light to go ahead with its work. And neither they nor anybody else ever asked us to do anything in the hospital that was dishonourable.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kvesic. I've completed my redirect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you wish to have the reference about the Hippocratic oath I've just looked it up. It is page 53, the question was on line 7 and then the following question was on line 13 of that same page. And my learned friend was quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, on behalf of my colleagues I'd like to thank you for having come to bring your testimony to the Stojic Defence, and I'd like to wish you all the best for your return to your country and of course in the continuation of your profession that you exercise currently. Thank you very much and may I ask the usher to kindly accompany you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe Mr. Stringer and Mr. Kovacic are going to take the floor, but before they take the floor, for next week we have two witnesses. One first witness, I'm not giving the witness's name, who is planned for two hours for direct examination, testifying Monday and Tuesday; and the second witness for two hours, testifying Wednesday and Thursday. So all of this is fixed. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but Mr. Stringer let me go first. Your Honours, I'm a little worried today, a little concerned because I seem to feel that the tragic event that took place at Schiphol airport today in Amsterdam might upset the arrival of our witness for tomorrow. I hope it doesn't, or, rather, the day after tomorrow. I hope it doesn't effect that but if there are any difficulties, I will let the Court know in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We must hope that the airport will function and that the flights will resume and that your witness will arrive. I don't think there's much concern to have on that account. Mr. Stringer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good evening to you and to Your Honours and counsel, and everyone else. Mr. President, I'm on my feet to request on behalf of the Prosecution the Trial Chamber's permission to make a brief oral reply to a written submission that was filed today by the all of the Defence. I'm referring to the joint Defence response to Prosecution motion seeking to exclude irrelevant evidence to be offered by a Bruno Stojic witness and the name of the witness who appears next Wednesday. I think he is open session but I'm not going to say his name just to be cautious. This is a response to a submission filed by the Prosecution last week on the 19th which relates to this witness, and the response of the Defence was filed today.
